scenarios.prompt: A client wants 20 minutes of activation before every session.
scenarios.goodAnswer: Keep a short warm-up; move strengthening into the main session with progressive load; make no claim that activation fixes anything.

lesson.title: Correctives and activation: what the evidence supports
lesson.summary: What exercise research on shoulder pain actually compared, how certain it is, and how to use activation drills as a warm-up rather than a fix.
objectives: Describe what research reports about exercise for subacromial and rotator cuff related shoulder pain, for whom, and how certain it is.
Explain why that clinical research is not a trainer's treatment plan.
Use activation drills as warm-up and rehearsal, without ranking them.
Know when a "corrective" should be a referral instead.

blocks.content: "Correctives" and "activation" are some of the most used words in shoulder training. This lesson separates what research tested from what is coaching practice, so you can use both honestly.
What research reports, and for whom

For subacromial shoulder pain, a specific condition that a clinician diagnoses, UK specialist guidance from the British Elbow & Shoulder Society reports evidence that exercise reduces pain over 8 weeks to 6 months and improves the function patients report, at follow-up of up to six months. It grades that recommendation as conditional and positive, on low evidence, and says the best physiotherapy, exercise or manual therapy approach is still uncertain.

For adults whose subacromial pain had lasted more than three months, a systematic review with meta-analysis found high-certainty evidence that surgery to decompress the space gave no additional benefit over placebo surgery, for pain at one year or for physical function at one to two years.

For rotator cuff related shoulder pain, a 2020 systematic review compared each kind of exercise with placebo or no treatment, not with each other, over more than six weeks and up to six months. Progressive and resisted exercise showed an uncertain clinical benefit; non-progressive or non-resisted exercise showed no significant benefit. The certainty of the evidence was low.

content.label: Spindle policy
content.text: Your training is not treatment for a diagnosed condition. A client with diagnosed shoulder pain, or one recovering from surgery, a dislocation or a fracture, trains within the treating clinician's plan, and you do not progress that plan on your own. This is Spindle's rule for trainers, not a research finding.

blocks.content: In a session, use activation drills as rehearsal and warm-up: a way to get the client's attention on a position before loading it. Do not present them as a fix, and keep them short.
Can the client hold the position you want under a light load, with smooth movement and no pain? Re-check the screen from lesson 4 the same way in a later session to see whether anything changed.

content.label: Stop and refer
content.text: If pain comes on or rises, or any warning sign appears: Stop shoulder loading for the rest of the session. Pain that is getting worse: routine referral now; do not wait. Pain that has not improved after 2 weeks: routine referral. A new inability to lift or move the arm themselves, without an injury: urgent, today. Pins and needles that do not go away, or no feeling in the arm or shoulder: urgent, today. This never clears anyone and never names an injury.

content.alt: Four schematic figures: standing with the back against a wall; seen from the front with the right elbow at the side and the forearm turned out against a band; reaching both arms forward; pressing one arm overhead with a light weight.
content.caption: A short warm-up, in order. Schematic, not to scale.

legend.label: Position.
legend.text: The stance or support of the first lift.

legend.label: Light rotation.
legend.text: Elbow at the side, forearm out and back.

legend.label: Shoulder blade control.

content: Position: set up the stance or support you will use in the first lift. Easier version: support the back against a wall or bench.
Light rotation: elbow at the side, turn the forearm out and back with a light band, 8 to 12 slow reps. Easier version: no band.
Shoulder blade control: reach the arms forward and let the shoulder blades travel around the ribs, then reach overhead along a wall. Easier version: reach only as high as is comfortable.
First pattern: the session's first press or pull with a light load, one to three cues only.

content.label: Stop and refer
content.text: If pain comes on or rises, or any warning sign appears: Stop shoulder loading for the rest of the session. A warm-up drill that hurts is not a warm-up: skip it. Pain that is getting worse: routine referral now; do not wait. Pain that has not improved after 2 weeks: routine referral. A new inability to lift or move the arm themselves, without an injury: urgent, today. This never clears anyone and never names an injury.

blocks.content: Give one to three cues per drill, as a direction or a target: "reach long through your hands", "push the band away". Watch the next rep, and keep a cue only if the movement changes the way you want.

content.label: Stop and refer
content.text: Correctives never replace referral. Any stop rule means: Stop shoulder loading for the rest of the session. Pain that is getting worse: routine referral now; do not wait. Pain that has not improved after 2 weeks: routine referral. Anything in the urgent or emergency tiers: refer at that tier (see "When to refer out").

content.prompt: What does UK specialist guidance report about exercise for subacromial shoulder pain?
options: It reduces pain over 8 weeks to 6 months and improves patient-reported function; the recommendation is conditional, on low evidence, and the best approach is uncertain
One exercise programme is proven best
content.explanation: The guidance reports that exercise reduces pain over 8 weeks to 6 months and improves patient-reported function, grades this conditional positive on low evidence, and says the best approach is still uncertain.

content.prompt: How did the 2020 review compare progressive and non-progressive exercise for rotator cuff related shoulder pain?
options: It found progressive exercise clearly better than non-progressive
It compared each with placebo or no treatment, not with each other, and the evidence was low certainty
It found no difference between them in a head-to-head comparison
content.explanation: Each approach was compared with placebo or no treatment over more than six weeks to six months; the review did not compare them head to head, and certainty was low.

content.label: Talk it through
content.text: A client wants to spend 20 minutes on activation before every session. What do you keep as a short warm-up, and what moves into the main session as real training?
